rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved separation while measuring the critical pair’s sensitivity to gradient slope.

The 8-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature one step to test whether retention can be shortened without sacrificing full resolution.

The temperature increase improved critical-pair resolution while shortening retention. Test a 6-minute gradient to locate the speed limit for full resolution, retaining injection 3 as a maximum-score fallback.

The critical pair lost resolution when the gradient steepened. Lowering phi1 to 0.75 restores nearly the successful 8-minute gradient’s slope within a shorter programmed gradient, while remaining above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that gave full resolution. This should reduce time spent below the elution window and shorten retention; the run will test whether the early pair and critical middle pair remain resolved.

Shift the window upward another grid step at constant slope to shorten retention further. Injection 6 preserves maximum CRF as a fallback if reduced initial retention pushes the critical pair below R = 1.5.

Raise temperature one step to recover the small critical-pair resolution deficit, since the earlier temperature increase improved that pair’s selectivity. This also tests a route to full resolution with a shorter last-peak time.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while keeping the endpoint fixed, making the gradient slightly shallower to help protect the critical pair. Monitor the early pair as well, since its resolution decreased at 50 C.

Move the starting composition upward another step while reducing the endpoint to make the gradient shallower and help preserve middle-pair resolution. This tests further time savings while checking whether the early peaks become too compressed.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to recover its small middle-pair resolution deficit. The trimmed endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition and allows a shorter programmed gradient.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a much steeper gradient for a potentially faster separation with a changed middle-pair elution order. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, and the high endpoint limits the risk of missing late compounds.

Explore a faster, high-starting-organic method at lower temperature to test a different selectivity regime for the unresolved middle pair. Cooling should help retain the early compounds despite the increased starting organic fraction; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction changes middle-pair selectivity enough to improve the fast separation. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed relative to injection 13, monitoring both early-peak compression and the unresolved late pair.

Test whether a further upward window shift improves the unresolved middle pair and brings the late pair above R = 1.5 in this fast regime. The first peak may approach the dead time, so early-pair resolution will also be a key check; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Narrow the gradient window at the same starting composition to test whether a shallower slope resolves the remaining middle pair in this fast selectivity regime. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition in injection 15.

The middle pair improved with a shallower gradient, so narrow the window further to seek full resolution. The late peaks may elute during the final hold, but the prior elution window suggests this endpoint is sufficient to avoid a truncated run.

Further slope reduction gave little middle-pair improvement, so test a higher starting composition for a selectivity change while restoring a stronger endpoint for rapid late elution. This probes the tradeoff between improved middle-pair separation and compression of the early pair.

Return to the starting composition that preserved early-pair resolution and test temperature-dependent selectivity for the unresolved middle pair. A 5 C increase isolates the temperature effect relative to injection 16 while potentially shortening late retention.

Return to the maximum-score region with a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin. Trimming the endpoint to 0.60 should keep all peaks within the gradient while reducing its programmed duration to 4 minutes.

Refine the fastest fully resolved method, injection 11, by lowering the endpoint one step to improve its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. The last peak should remain within the gradient, with only a modest retention-time increase and no time penalty expected.

Test a higher starting composition for shorter retention, offsetting early-peak compression by cooling one temperature step. The narrower, shallower gradient may help preserve middle-pair resolution; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Refine around injection 11 with a slope between those of injections 11 and 21, targeting full resolution with more margin than injection 11 and less retention than injection 21. Maximum CRF is already secured, so this tests a practical speed–resolution compromise.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a narrower window around injection 20 to improve the minimum resolution margin while keeping a short programmed gradient. The last peak should still elute within the gradient and comfortably before the time penalty begins.

Preserve injection 11’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while extending to a stronger endpoint for column cleanup. This should reproduce its fast, fully resolved elution pattern and retain the maximum CRF already achieved.
